props.title: Starting Out in the Evening

sections.content: Starting Out in the Evening (2007) stands as a masterful character study of literary ambition and late-life reckoning. Frank Langella delivers a career-defining performance as aging novelist Leonard Schiller, reminiscent of the quiet dignity found in The Straight Story (1999) and the intellectual wrestling of Wonder Boys (2000). The film's intimate exploration of a writer facing mortality recalls Shadowlands (1993), though with a more contemporary New York literary scene backdrop. Director Andrew Wagner crafts a delicate meditation on art, aging, and the price of dedication to craft.

sections.content: The film's central relationship between Schiller and graduate student Heather Wolfe (Lauren Ambrose) echoes similar May-December intellectual partnerships in cinema, though with greater nuance than Elegy (2008) or The Squid and the Whale (2005). Wagner's direction emphasizes the quiet moments - the sound of typewriter keys, lingering shots of book-lined apartments, the weight of silence between conversations. This approach aligns with other literary-minded films like Can You Ever Forgive Me? (2018) and Capote (2005), where the solitary nature of writing becomes almost tangible.

The subplot involving Schiller's daughter Ariel (Lili Taylor) adds crucial depth to the exploration of life choices and artistic sacrifice. Like The Wife (2017) and Bright Star (2009), the film examines how devotion to literature affects personal relationships. The muted color palette and careful pacing create an autumn-like atmosphere that perfectly matches the story's themes of late-life reflection and potential renewal. SUBHEAD: Literary Lives on Screen

sections.content: Wagner's film belongs to a rich tradition of movies exploring the writer's life, though it avoids the typical tropes of alcoholism and dramatic creative breakthroughs seen in films like Barton Fink (1991) or Adaptation (2002). Instead, it shares more DNA with quieter examinations like The Hours (2002) and Bright Star (2009), where the creative process is portrayed as a gradual, often painful evolution rather than sudden inspiration.
